seo.title: Root Rot in Houseplants: Signs and Rescue Steps (2026)
seo.description: Root rot: spot it from the wilt, smell and soft brown roots, then trim, repot smaller or save cuttings depending on the damage. Free rescue planner. 2026 guide.
seo.h1: Root rot in houseplants: how to spot it and save the plant

answer: Root rot shows as wilting in wet mix, a sour smell, and roots that are brown to black and soft instead of firm. Unpot the plant, rinse the roots, cut every rotten one back to firm tissue and repot in fresh, sterile mix. If most roots are dead, root cuttings instead.
intro: Root rot is the stage where too much water stops being a care mistake and becomes an infection. Soil fungi such as Pythium, Phytophthora and Rhizoctonia live in potting mix and plant debris, and Clemson Cooperative Extension explains that overwatering increases how often they take hold, because roots sitting in saturated mix are already short of oxygen and weakened. Once infected, the roots turn brown to black and soft, stop absorbing water, and the plant wilts even though the pot is wet. Above ground, it can look like simple thirst for weeks. Below ground, the damage spreads root by root, and a ring of dark tissue can eventually girdle the stem at the soil line. Whether a plant can be saved depends almost entirely on how much healthy root is left, which you can only learn by taking it out of the pot. This guide shows how to judge that, what to cut, which pot to use for recovery, and when cuttings are the better bet.

tool.title: Enter the share of rotten roots, whether firm stems remain and your pot size: the planner gives a rescue plan.

paras: Rot rarely announces itself at the roots, because nobody looks there until the plant is in trouble. The first clues are a wilt that does not lift when the mix is wet, leaves yellowing several at a time, a sour or rotten smell from the pot, and stems that feel soft at the base. Clemson describes stems girdled at or near soil level by a ring of brown or black tissue, and infected roots that are brown to black and may be soft. Fungus gnats hovering over the soil are a hint that the mix stays too wet; Clemson notes their larvae can also feed on roots.
Plants with storage organs show it in their own way, and the plant guides on this site describe each one.

paras: Clemson's method for removing a plant is to turn the pot upside down, hold the soil back with your hand, the stem between two fingers, and knock the rim against something solid until the root ball slides out. Large plants may need the pot cut or laid on its side.

Rinse the old mix off the roots under lukewarm water so you can see them. Healthy roots are firm and pale; rotten ones are brown to black, soft, and often break apart when you squeeze them. Now estimate the share of the root system that is rotten. That one number is what the planner above needs, along with whether the stems are still firm and the current pot diameter.

sections.h2: Matching the rescue to the rot
paras: Clemson gives the two ends of the scale. If only a few roots are infected, cut them out and repot in sterile soil. If most roots are dark, soft and dead, it is better to discard the plant. The planner fills in the middle ground with cutoffs at 25 and 75 percent. Those cutoffs are our rule of thumb for turning Clemson's advice into steps, not a figure any extension service publishes.

The middle band is where judgment counts. A plant that has lost half its roots still carries all its leaves, and they keep losing water faster than the surviving roots can replace it; trimming some foliage restores the balance. The smaller pot follows the same logic: a pot sized for the old root system holds far more mix than the survivors can dry out, so it stays wet and the rot returns. Taking two or three stem cuttings at the same time costs nothing and gives you a fallback if the parent fails. Choose firm pieces well above any dark tissue and root them in water or barely damp mix.

sections.h2: Cutting and repotting, step by step
paras: Work quickly once the roots are bare, and keep everything that touched the old mix away from your other plants.
list: Cut every brown, soft root back to firm tissue with clean, sharp shears, wiping the blades between cuts.
For rhizomes, tubers and succulent stems, let the cut surfaces dry before replanting: the snake plant guide gives a day, the succulent guide a few days.
Throw away the old mix. Clemson says the rot fungi survive in soil and debris, and spores spread with splashing water and moved soil.
Scrub the pot and rinse it in one part bleach to nine parts water, the solution Clemson recommends for reused pots, or use a new pot with a drainage hole.

Repot in fresh, sterile potting mix at the same depth the plant grew before. A loose foliage mix drains better than heavy peat; Clemson suggests blends such as one part peat, one part pine bark and one part perlite.
If more than a quarter of the roots went, trim back some leaves too, so the smaller root system has less foliage to supply.
Water once lightly to settle the mix, then wait until it dries to the depth the plant's guide recommends.

paras: A plant that has just lost roots cannot drink much, so treat it gently. Keep it in bright, indirect light, never direct sun, and in normal room warmth: the Illinois Extension puts most foliage plants at 65 to 75 degrees by day. Skip fertilizer until new growth appears; the Illinois Extension says to feed only plants that are actively growing, and damaged roots are easily burned by salts.

Expect some wilting and a few more lost leaves while new roots form. Resist the urge to water a drooping plant whose mix is still damp, since that is exactly how the rot began. Fresh leaves or shoots are the sign of success. If the stems keep softening or the collapse continues, take cuttings from whatever is still firm before it is too late.

Fungicides for root and stem rot exist, but Clemson's verdict is practical: for most indoor gardeners they probably cost more than a new plant. They also do nothing for roots that are already dead. Cutting away the rot, replacing the mix and fixing the watering do the real work. Sterile mix matters more than any product, because garden soil carries the organisms that cause rot; Clemson notes that garden soil must be pasteurized before it can be used in pots, and that bagged soilless mixes are sterile from the start.

Every rescue is wasted if the conditions stay the same. Use pots with drainage holes and empty the saucer or cover pot after each watering. Do not put a layer of gravel or broken pot in the bottom: Clemson says it actually slows water movement through the pot. Choose a pot only 1 or 2 inches wider than the root ball when you repot, as Clemson advises, because a large volume of mix around a small root system stays wet for a long time.

Water by the feel of the mix, not by the calendar. Our overwatering vs underwatering guide covers the signs to check, and the guide to how often to water plants estimates a rhythm for your pot, light and season. When you buy a plant, check its roots before buying if you can; Clemson's first rule of disease control is to start with disease-free plants.

faq.q: Can a plant with root rot be saved?
faq.a: Yes, if enough healthy root remains. Clemson says a plant with only a few infected roots can be saved by cutting them out and repotting in sterile soil, but one whose roots are mostly dark, soft and dead is better discarded. In between, the odds depend on the plant and on aftercare. Even when the roots are lost, firm stems or leaves above the rot can often be rooted as cuttings, which keeps the plant going.

faq.q: Can I reuse the soil from a plant with root rot?
faq.a: No. Clemson explains that the fungi behind root and stem rot survive in the soil and in infected plant debris, so old mix carries the problem into the next planting. Bag it and throw it out rather than adding it to other pots. Use fresh, sterile potting mix, and clean the pot before reusing it by scrubbing it and rinsing it in one part bleach to nine parts water.

faq.q: Should I use a fungicide on a plant with root rot?
faq.a: Usually not. Clemson notes that fungicides for root rot are available but that for most indoor gardeners they will probably cost more than a new plant, and they cannot revive roots that are already dead. The effective treatment is mechanical: unpot, cut away rotten roots, discard the old mix, disinfect the pot and replant in sterile mix. Then change the watering habits and drainage that let the rot start.

faq.q: What do healthy roots look like compared with rotten ones?
faq.a: Healthy roots are firm, springy and pale, often white or cream, with fine root hairs on the youngest tips. Rotten roots are brown to black, as Clemson describes them, soft or mushy, and break or come apart when pinched. A sour or rotten smell usually comes with them. Some plants have naturally darker roots, so judge by firmness as much as color, and compare the suspect roots with the newest ones near the surface.

faq.q: Why did my plant get root rot in a pot with drainage holes?
faq.a: A hole only lets water out if the mix lets it through. Dense, peat-heavy mixes hold water for a long time, as Clemson notes, and so does a pot far larger than the root ball. A saucer or cover pot holding drained water keeps the bottom roots soaked, and a gravel layer slows drainage instead of helping. Cool, dim spots dry slowly. Combine any of these with frequent watering and roots stay saturated.
